newsitem.title: USA: Choosing the best Internet provider for you.
newsitem.headline: Choosing the best Internet provider for you.

text.p: Pity the poor souls who're just looking into this "Internet thing."
Their timing couldn't be worse.

The country's biggest Internet provider, America Online, is one big traffic jam, and at present, has stopped advertising for new subscribers. Other major Internet on-ramps, including CompuServe and Netcom On-Line Communications, have ceded their consumer Internet business to America Online and are courting business customers exclusively.
Meanwhile, the number of independent Internet providers doing business in the United States and Canada has by some estimates jumped to more than 4,000.
How does somebody who knows next to nothing about going online figure out the best way to get there?

"That is the most common question I'm asked," said Gary Gach, an Internet trainer at the University of California, the Learning Annex in Berkeley, Calif., and author of "The Pocket Guide to the Internet."
"What I tell people is if there were one good provider, there wouldn't be competition," he said.

Trainers and consumer advocates recommend treating your search for an Internet provider as you would any other shopping expedition: figure out what you need, find out what's available, then look for the best match.

"When you go grocery shopping, you make a list. You need to use the same approach when you shop for (Internet) providers," said Cleo Manuel, public affairs vice president with the National Consumers League.
According to the experts, finding a provider that suits you boils down to a few essentials:

-- Community and content -- Networks such as America Online package Internet access with original content, as well as message boards and chat rooms where subscribers can converse. A few Internet providers offer similar community-building extras, but most offer a bare-bone connection to the Internet, and assume subscribers will do their socializing on the discussion groups known as newsgroups, as well as Web sites and electronic mailing lists.

-- Price -- A flat monthly fee of $19.95 for unlimited access has become the industry standard, but it might not suit everyone. People who don't expect to be online more than a few hours a month might do better by paying less for limited access. People with special interests might be willing to pay extra for access to otherwise hard-to-get information. To find out if you'll get your money's worth, take advantage of the 30-day free trial offers many companies offer, Gach said. Consider phone costs as well, he said. If dialing into an Internet provider isn't a local call, the extra toll charges could add up.

-- Access -- Most Internet providers offer today's standard modem speed of 28 kilobits per second and many offer faster, more expensive ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) lines. But fast connections don't mean anything if you can't log on. According to Boardwatch Magazine, the average Internet provider has approximately nine customers per modem. Much more than that and you could run into busy signals, experts caution. Frequent travelers who want to log on from the road might want to consider using a national service with dial-in numbers across the country, or the world, they said.

-- Customer service -- Internet providers offer varying levels of support, including answers to frequently asked questions, or FAQs, on the company's Web site; live online chats with technicians; e-mail help desks and a 24-hour, seven-day telephone crew. It pays to find out what the companies you're investigating offer "because sometimes you prefer one thing but they prefer another," Gach said. One way to gauge support: ask friends or family who are already online about their experiences, he said.

-- Software -- Some providers start you off with all the basics, including programmes for sending and receiving e-mail, browsing the Web, posting to newsgroups and downloading files. Others provide the connection and leave subscribers to gather their own software. "If that's the kind of thing that makes you run screaming, you might want to choose a provider" with a prepackaged software suite, Gach said.

The National Consumers League's brochure, "Making Sense of Your New Communications Choices," includes guidelines for selecting an Internet provider and is available online (http://www.gte.com/nclbroch/index.html) or by calling (800) 355-9NCL (9625).
Some places to start looking for Internet providers:

-- The List (http://thelist.iworld.com/) -- A comprehensive index of 4,504 Internet providers worldwide searchable by name or geography. Listings include area covered, phone numbers, e-mail addresses, services, and rates.

-- cnet's ISP comparison (http://www.cnet.com/Content/Reviews/Compare/ISP) -- Reader ratings of 608 mostly U.S. Internet providers, some of which are also reviewed by staff at the cnet Internet publication. The latter include area covered, phone numbers, services and rates.

-- Boardwatch's Internet service providers directory (http://www.boardwatch.com/isp/index.htm) - An index of 3,068 U.S. Internet providers set up with a map interface. Listings include area covered, phone numbers, total number of dial-in ports and rates. Print copies of the directory cost $13.95 and are available by writing Boardwatch Magazine, 8500 W. Bowles Ave., Suite 210, Littleton, Colo., 80123.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
